title: “TRAIN UP A CHILD”—AND HE STILL WALKED AWAY: DID GOD BREAK HIS PROMISE?
paragraphs: “TRAIN UP A CHILD”—AND HE STILL WALKED AWAY: DID GOD BREAK HIS PROMISE?
What Proverbs 22:6 Really Says to the Parent Who Did Everything They Knew to Do… and Is Still Waiting for Their Child to Come Home
There is a particular kind of heartbreak that happens quietly.
No funeral.
No hospital room.
No sympathy cards arriving at the door.
Just an empty chair.
A bedroom that does not feel the same anymore.
A Bible you once bought for a child whose hands no longer open it.
A mother scrolling through photographs from years ago, stopping at the one where her little boy was smiling in church.
A father remembering the night his daughter folded tiny hands beside her bed and whispered a prayer to Jesus.
You taught them Scripture.
You brought them to church.
You prayed over them.
You corrected them.
You forgave them.
You tried to model Christ.
You failed sometimes too—and those failures still visit you at two in the morning.
But you tried.
And now?
Maybe they want nothing to do with God.
Maybe they laugh at what they once believed.
Maybe they are living in a way that terrifies you.
Maybe they still call themselves Christian, but Christ seems to have become a distant accessory rather than Lord.
And somewhere in the middle of all that grief, someone quotes the verse.
“Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.”
Proverbs 22:6.
And suddenly a verse that was supposed to comfort you feels almost like an accusation.
So you begin asking questions you are afraid to say aloud.
Did I fail?
Did I not pray enough?
Was my faith fake?
Did I somehow ruin my child?
And perhaps the question underneath every other question is even harder:
Did God promise me something He has not done?
That is where we need to stop repeating Proverbs 22:6 like a Christian slogan and actually listen to what Scripture says.
Because God does not need us to exaggerate His Word in order to defend Him.
The Hebrew text reads:
חֲנֹךְ לַנַּעַר עַל־פִּי דַרְכּוֹ גַּם כִּי־יַזְקִין לֹא־יָסוּר מִמֶּנָּה׃
Ḥănōḵ lannaʿar ʿal-pî darkô; gam kî-yazqîn, lō-yāsûr mimmennāh.
Traditionally:
“Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.”
But there is more happening underneath the English than many of us realize.
The opening word, חֲנֹךְ—ḥănōḵ—comes from the Hebrew verb חנך, ḥānak.
It carries the idea of training, initiating, or dedicating.
That matters.
Biblical parenting is not merely controlling behavior long enough to produce a respectable adult.
It is formation.
Dedication.
Direction.
It is repeatedly placing truth before a young human heart while knowing that you cannot climb inside that heart and make it worship God.
And the person being trained is called הַנַּעַר—hannaʿar.
Naʿar can describe a child or youth across a surprisingly broad range of young life.
Then comes the phrase that has produced enormous discussion:
עַל־פִּי דַרְכּוֹ
ʿal-pî darkô.
Literally, something close to “according to the mouth of his way,” an idiomatic expression commonly understood along the lines of “according to his way.”
Some have interpreted this as training a child according to his individual disposition, temperament, or natural bent.
That may contain useful parenting wisdom, but we should be careful about claiming that this is certainly what Solomon meant.
Within Proverbs, “way” is deeply moral.
There is a way of wisdom.
A way of righteousness.
A way of folly.
A way that appears right to a person yet ends in death.
Proverbs is relentlessly concerned with which road a human being walks.
So Proverbs 22:6 is not giving parents a magical technique for programming children.
It is wisdom about formation.
Set the young person upon the path.
Teach.
Correct.
Model.
Repeat.
Live the truth in front of them.
Make wisdom familiar.
Make righteousness a road their feet know well.
And here is where devastated parents need to hear something that may remove years of unnecessary shame:
A proverb is not the same literary form as an unconditional covenant promise.
Proverbs gives us wisdom—truthful observations about the way God has ordered life and the ordinary consequences of wisdom and foolishness.
Consider other proverbs.
Proverbs teaches that diligent hands tend toward prosperity.
That is true.
But Scripture also contains righteous people who suffer poverty.
Proverbs teaches that a gentle answer turns away wrath.
That is true.
But sometimes you can answer gently and the angry person becomes angrier anyway.
Why?
Because Proverbs teaches wisdom for living in God's world. It is not presenting every maxim as a mechanical formula that eliminates human choice, suffering, providence, or every possible exception.
And that changes how we hear Proverbs 22:6.
It gives parents enormous reason to take spiritual formation seriously.
What children repeatedly receive matters.
What they repeatedly watch matters.
What becomes normal in their home matters.
The prayers matter.
The conversations matter.
The apologies matter.
The correction matters.
The nights when you are exhausted but sit beside the bed anyway matter.
The Sunday mornings when getting everyone out the door feels like a small military campaign matter.
The moments when your child catches you praying when you did not know anyone was watching matter.
But the proverb should not be weaponized against a grieving mother or father as though an adult child's rebellion mathematically proves parental failure.
Because your child is not a machine.
Your child bears the dignity—and terrible responsibility—of being a human being who makes real moral choices before God.
Think about Scripture itself.
God's Word never hides the scandals inside families.
Adam had Cain.
Isaac had Esau.
Samuel's sons did not walk in his ways.
David's household became a landscape of terrible consequences, sin, grief, violence, rebellion, and regret.
Scripture refuses to give us sanitized families.
And maybe that is because God knew we would eventually need a Bible honest enough to survive our own homes.
Some parents need to hear this with tears running down their faces:
Your child's present rebellion does not automatically prove that every seed you planted was worthless.
And it certainly does not mean you should stop praying.
Seeds can disappear beneath the soil long before anything green appears above it.
But we must be equally careful here.
We cannot turn Proverbs 22:6 into another guarantee by saying, “Don't worry. Every wandering child definitely returns before death.”
Scripture does not give us permission to promise that either.
We pray.
We plead.
We love.
We speak truth.
We keep the door of appropriate reconciliation open.
We trust God's power.
But salvation belongs to the Lord.
No parent can repent on behalf of an adult child.
No mother can believe the Gospel for her son.
No father can surrender his daughter's heart to Christ in her place.
Christian parents are called to faithfulness.
They are not granted sovereignty.
And strangely enough, that truth can become freedom.
Because some of you have been trying to carry a responsibility that belongs to God.
You replay everything.
Maybe if I had been more patient.
Maybe if I had disciplined differently.
Maybe if we had chosen another church.
Maybe if I had noticed sooner.
Maybe if I had worked less.
Maybe if I had prayed more.
Maybe.
Maybe.
Maybe.
There may indeed be things to repent of.
Good parents are still sinners.
Sometimes our children carry wounds connected to things we did.
When that is true, Christianity does not teach us to hide behind Proverbs 22:6.
It teaches us to confess.
To apologize without excuses.
To seek forgiveness.
To make restitution where appropriate.
To say the words some parents find almost impossible to say:
“I was wrong.”
That can be holy ground.
But repentance is different from endless self-condemnation.
The Gospel does not ask you to pretend you were a perfect parent.
It tells you something infinitely better.
There is a perfect Savior for imperfect parents.
Jesus Christ did not go to the cross because respectable Christian families had managed to get everything right.
He went because none of us had.
Parents need grace.
Children need grace.
Prodigals need grace.
Preachers need grace.
The son who ran away needs grace.
The mother crying in the kitchen needs grace.
The father wondering where he went wrong needs grace.
And the child who grew up in church but learned how to hide sin beneath Christian language needs grace too.
This is why the deepest answer to Proverbs 22:6 is not a parenting technique.
It is Jesus Christ.
Parenting can expose a child to truth.
Parenting can model truth.
Parenting can teach truth.
Parenting can discipline toward wisdom.
But parenting cannot regenerate a human heart.
Only God saves.
That realization should not make parents passive.
It should drive them to their knees.
Teach your children about Jesus.
Not merely how to behave in church.
Jesus.
Teach them why sin is deadly.
Teach them why grace is astonishing.
Teach them that repentance is not humiliation before an angry God but turning from sin toward the God who calls sinners home.
Let them see that Christianity is not Dad pretending he never struggles.
It is Dad repenting when he sins.
It is not Mom maintaining the appearance of the perfect Christian household.
It is Mom depending upon Christ when the household is breaking her heart.
Let them discover that the Gospel is strong enough for questions.
Strong enough for failure.
Strong enough for confession.
Strong enough for shame.
Strong enough for scandal.
Strong enough for the day somebody in the family does the thing nobody imagined they would ever do.
Because this is what Jesus does.
He walks into stories human beings think are already ruined.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted His people.
The thief beside Him had no lifetime left in which to repair his reputation.
Yet grace kept writing.
That does not make sin insignificant.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion does not matter.
Look at the cross.
Sin mattered enough for the Son of God to bleed.
But look again at the cross.
The sinner mattered enough for the Son of God to bleed.
That is the Gospel.
So if your child is wandering tonight, pray.
Do not pray merely, “God, make my child behave again.”
Pray for resurrection.
“Jesus, reveal Yourself to them.”
“Convict them.”
“Protect them from deception.”
“Bring people into their life who will speak truth.”
“Destroy the lies they have believed.”
“Give me wisdom to know when to speak and when to remain quiet.”
“Show me anything in myself that needs repentance.”
“And Lord, do what I cannot do.”
Then love them without calling darkness light.
Grace does not require approving what God calls sin.
Truth does not require becoming cruel.
Jesus was full of grace and truth.
Christian parents are called toward that same difficult intersection.
And if you are reading this as the child rather than the parent—perhaps you are the one who walked away—listen carefully.
Your mother's prayers cannot save you.
Your father's faith cannot save you.
Your Christian childhood cannot save you.
Being baptized years ago cannot substitute for knowing Christ.
Having Bible verses buried somewhere in your memory is not the same thing as surrendering your life to Jesus.
Maybe you have spent years running because Christianity became tangled in your mind with hypocrisy, pain, control, disappointment, or people who represented Jesus badly.
What happened to you matters.
But the failures of Christians do not change who Christ is.
Do not reject Jesus because somebody wearing His name wounded you.
Look at Him for yourself.
Look at the Christ who touched lepers.
Look at the Christ who ate with sinners.
Look at the Christ who confronted religious hypocrisy.
Look at the Christ who welcomed the broken.
Look at the Christ who carried a cross.
Look at the empty tomb.
Then decide what you will do with Him.
Maybe Proverbs 22:6 has been sitting somewhere inside you for years.
Maybe you remember Scripture you thought you had forgotten.
A hymn suddenly returns.
A sentence from your grandmother.
Your father's voice praying.
Your mother's Bible open on the table.
A Sunday school teacher saying the name Jesus.
Do not confuse those memories with salvation.
But do not dismiss them either.
Perhaps someone planted.
Someone watered.
And even now, God is confronting you with the Gospel again.
Come home to Christ.
Not merely to church culture.
Not merely to your parents.
Not merely to the person you used to be.
To Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Stop negotiating with the sin that is destroying you.
Stop assuming there will always be another year.
Jesus still receives sinners.
And perhaps that is the sentence someone reading this desperately needed tonight.
Jesus still receives sinners.
Someone else reading may realize they are not alone because you were brave enough to say it.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
There may be a father secretly wondering whether God broke His promise.
Jesus Christ.
And not because anyone should manipulate you into giving.
Scripture says giving should come from the heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But voluntary generosity can genuinely help Christian ministry continue.
Your giving does not buy grace.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
Your support simply helps put the message of that grace in front of another human being who may desperately need to hear it.
So what does Proverbs 22:6 ultimately leave us with?
Not a formula.
Not permission for careless parenting.
Not a weapon for condemning grieving parents.
And not an excuse to stop praying.
It leaves us with wisdom.
Train them.
Teach them.
Dedicate yourself to showing them the way of truth.
Repent when you fail.
Keep praying when they wander.
Keep believing that no sinner is beyond the reach of Christ.
And leave the throne to God.
Maybe you are staring at an unfinished story.
Good.
Then do not write “The End” where God has placed only a comma.
You do not know what the next phone call will contain.
You do not know what conviction may already be stirring in a heart far away.
You do not know what remembered Scripture may return in the middle of somebody's darkest night.
You do not know what God may yet do.
But you know who Jesus is.
And sometimes faith is simply refusing to mistake the chapter you are crying through for the final page.
The child may have wandered far from the road you showed them—but Jesus has never lost the address.
